summary: 7a continues the hutrah/dchuya dispute framed on 6b (Rav Nachman: hutrah; Rav Sheshet: dchuya). Rav Sheshet opens with a proof for dchuya from the omer baraita; three further anonymous objections (מיתיבי / ת״ש) then press the same direction, from the meal-offering baraita, the blood-sprinkling rule, and the tzitz atonement list. Rav Nachman answers Rav Sheshet's proof and two of the objections by identifying a distinct technical factor unrelated to hutrah/dchuya, and the anonymous Gemara answers the blood-sprinkling objection the same way, on his behalf. The omer case: there are eating-remnants, a separate concern that always requires purity regardless of hutrah/dchuya. The meal-offering objection: Rav Nachman reassigns each listed sacrifice to a different explaining factor - the par avodah zarah has no fixed time, Aaron's ram is an individual's offering, and the omer lamb has eating-remnants like the first case. The blood-sprinkling ruling: the anonymous Gemara answers that it concerns an individual, not a communal offering. The tzitz objection: Rav Nachman answers that the clause means an individual's offering (a communal one needs no tzitz at all, since impurity is simply permitted for it), or, if it does mean a communal offering, one without a fixed time. The page closes with a new objection from the tzitz's own atonement verse: what sin does it address? Not piggul and not notar, both already excluded by their own pesukim. The Gemara's text breaks off mid-sentence after the complete word 'הא', before naming the remaining sin; Rashi notes the comment is completed on 7b.

display.title: Rav Sheshet's proof and three anonymous objections press dchuya; Rav Nachman's side answers each; tzitz sin-scope opens
display.oneLine: Rav Sheshet's proof and three further anonymous objections press dchuya from four baraitot; Rav Nachman, and for one objection the anonymous Gemara on his behalf, answers each case-by-case; the tzitz's own atonement verse then opens a new objection - which sin does the tzitz bear, if not piggul and not notar - that the daf leaves unresolved, breaking off mid-sentence after the complete word 'הא'.
display.shortSummary: Rav Sheshet's proof from the omer baraita: the priest searches for a replacement when possible, suggesting dchuya (prohibition still exists, minimize it). Rav Nachman's answer: the omer has eating-remnants, which is a separate reason to seek purity regardless of the tumas meit rule. Second challenge, an anonymous objection (מיתיבי), from the meal-offering baraita (bulls, rams, sheep): same structure. Rav Nachman assigns each of the three categories to a case outside the true communal-fixed-time class: the par avodah zarah (bull for communal idol worship) has no fixed time; Aaron's ram is an individual's offering; the lamb with the omer has eating-remnants. Third challenge, an anonymous objection (מיתיבי), from the blood-sprinkling ruling: sprinkling impure blood on the altar is accepted beshogeg (unwittingly) but not bmezid (intentionally) - if hutrah, why the distinction? That ruling concerns an individual's offering, not communal - unattributed in the raw text, falling outside the communal hutrah/dchuya dispute either way. Fourth challenge, an anonymous objection (ת״ש), from the tzitz baraita: the frontplate effects acceptance 'whether individual or communal' - if hutrah for the tzibbur, why would the tzitz be needed at all for communal impurity? Rav Nachman answers in two stages: (1) the tzitz clause is about an individual - a communal offering needs no tzitz, since impurity is simply a permission (heter) for it; (2) or, granting it does mean a communal offering, it is limited to offerings without a fixed time. The page closes with a new objection: the tzitz verse says Aaron 'shall bear the sin' of the sacred things - which sin? Not piggul (the Torah already says it 'will not be accepted') and not notar (the Torah already says it 'will not be credited'). The daf's text breaks off mid-sentence after the complete word 'הא', before naming what remains; Rashi notes the comment is completed on 7b.
display.whats: The debate continues as a point-by-point contest, continuing the dispute stated on 6b: Rav Nachman holds tumas meit btzibur is hutrah (fully permitted); Rav Sheshet holds it is dchuya (overridden by necessity, minimized wherever possible). Rav Sheshet opens with a proof from the omer baraita; three further anonymous objections then press the same direction, citing baraitot that show the system treats tumas meit as if a prohibition still exists (finding replacements, conditional acceptance, a needed atonement). Rav Nachman's strategy: in each case, identify a technical factor that explains the ruling without conceding dchuya; the anonymous Gemara answers the blood-sprinkling objection the same way, on his behalf. The final objection - from the tzitz baraita - is the most direct challenge, because it explicitly includes 'tzibbur' among the cases the tzitz's acceptance covers; if tumas meit in tzibbur were simply permitted, the tzitz should have nothing to do for it. Rav Nachman answers that the clause either means an individual, or a communal offering without a fixed time. The tzitz-sin-scope objection that follows presses further: the verse frames the tzitz's function as bearing a sin - by elimination, not piggul, not notar - but the daf ends before the Gemara says what sin remains or what that implies for hutrah versus dchuya.
display.hint: If every objection on this daf is answered, why does the sugya still end on an open, unresolved challenge instead of a resolution?

learning.learnerQuestion: Rav Sheshet's proof, plus three further anonymous objections, all press dchuya. Every one is answered - three times by Rav Nachman himself, once by the anonymous Gemara on his behalf. Who is winning this debate?
learning.coreTension: Rav Sheshet's proof and the anonymous objections that follow it all point the same direction: the system treats tumas meit in tzibbur as a prohibited act that must be minimized wherever possible, not simply ignored. Rav Nachman's answers are individually valid but each one narrows what his hutrah position still covers - he concedes cases where purity is required for unrelated reasons (eating-remnants), cases that are not really communal (individual offerings), and cases that are not really fixed-time. The question is whether the combination of concessions still leaves a coherent hutrah position, or amounts in practice to dchuya.
learning.coreMove: Track the three grounds used on Rav Nachman's side to push each challenge outside the disputed class: (1) eating-remnants (the omer, and the omer's lamb in the meal-offering baraita) - purity is required, but for a reason unrelated to hutrah/dchuya. (2) individual offerings (Aaron's ram, answered by Rav Nachman himself; the blood-sprinkling baraita, answered by the anonymous Gemara on his behalf) - these fall outside the communal hutrah/dchuya dispute entirely, proving nothing either way. (3) communal offerings without a fixed time (the par avodah zarah; the tzitz's residual case) - the tzitz may still be needed for them. After all four challenges are answered, hutrah applies, in Rav Nachman's account, only to: true communal offerings with a fixed time, where there are no eating-remnants.
learning.resolution: The debate is unresolved on this daf. A new objection opens from the tzitz's own atonement verse: 'Aaron shall bear the sin of the sacred things.' Which sin does the tzitz address? Not piggul - already excluded by its own pasuk ('it will not be accepted'). Not notar - already excluded by its own pasuk ('it will not be credited'). By elimination the Gemara appears to be narrowing toward tumah, but the text breaks off mid-sentence after the complete word 'הא', before saying so, and Rashi notes explicitly that this comment is completed on 7b. What the answer implies for hutrah versus dchuya is not stated here.

takeaway.text: A position can answer every individual objection and still look strained for it: each answer given on Rav Nachman's behalf to the four dchuya challenges is textually defensible, but stacking four separate reclassifications to preserve one ruling is itself evidence worth weighing - and the sugya does not let Rav Nachman close the case before raising one more open challenge.

reasoningPattern.notes: After each dchuya challenge - Rav Sheshet's opening proof and the three anonymous objections - the hutrah side narrows which cases still count as a genuine test of hutrah, until only true communal fixed-time offerings with no eating-remnants remain covered. Whether such a case is common in practice, and whether the final, unresolved tzitz-atonement objection undoes even that narrow residue, are the questions the sugya leaves open into 7b.

learning.ahaMoment: Rav Nachman's answer to the meal-offering baraita is the most instructive: he disaggregates 'bulls, rams, sheep' into three completely different sacrificial categories - par avodah zarah, Aaron's ram, and the omer lamb - each of which falls outside the true communal-fixed-time class for a different reason. This is not evasion; it is precise taxonomic work showing the baraita was never describing the case hutrah and dchuya actually dispute.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may think that because Rav Nachman keeps having to answer new challenges, his answers are gradually conceding ground to dchuya. Rav Nachman genuinely is being challenged - four real proofs and objections are raised against him - but each answer is a successful defense that keeps hutrah intact for the true case, not a concession that dchuya is correct.
learning.memoryAnchor: Nachman = hutrah, Sheshet = dchuya (from 6b). One proof, three anonymous objections, four answers: (1) omer - eating-remnants, unrelated to hutrah/dchuya. (2) par/ram/lamb - no fixed time, individual, and eating-remnants respectively, none a genuine test case. (3) blood shogeg/mezid - about an individual. (4) tzitz lists tzibbur - Nachman answers it means an individual, or (if communal) only offerings without a fixed time. New objection: tzitz 'bears a sin' - not piggul, not notar - daf ends before naming what remains; continues on 7b.

argumentFlow.label: Rav Sheshet: omer baraita proves dchuya
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Sheshet
argumentFlow.text: A baraita: if the omer meal-offering became impure while being sacrificed, the priest says so and a replacement is brought. Only if there is no replacement do they say 'be shrewd and keep silent.' This shows that when purity is possible, it is preferred - proving dchuya (the prohibition still operates and is minimized).

sourceRefs.note: Rav Sheshet's proof from the omer baraita

argumentFlow.label: Rav Nachman: omer case is eating-remnants, not the hutrah/dchuya question
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Nachman
argumentFlow.text: 'I concede where there are leftover portions to eat.' The omer's leftover minhah must be eaten by the priests, and remainders must be eaten in purity regardless of the tumas meit question - so seeking a replacement here proves nothing about hutrah or dchuya either way.

sourceRefs.note: Rav Nachman's concession, limited to this specific baraita

argumentFlow.label: Anonymous objection: meal-offering of bulls/rams/sheep proves dchuya
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: A second baraita: if the meal-offering accompanying bulls, rams, or sheep became impure, the same rule applies - bring a replacement if available.

sourceRefs.note: Anonymous objection (מיתיבי) from the meal-offering baraita, continuing the dchuya challenge

argumentFlow.label: Rav Nachman disaggregates bulls/rams/sheep into three non-qualifying cases
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Nachman
argumentFlow.text: Bulls = the par avodah zarah (the communal idol-worship atonement offering), which has no fixed time, so seeking a replacement is unremarkable. Rams = Aaron's own ram on Yom Kippur, an individual's offering, not communal. Sheep = specifically the lamb accompanying the omer (not the general libation-minchah of a sheep-offering, which is entirely burned with no remainder to require this distinction) - the omer's own minchah has eating-remnants. None of these is a true communal-fixed-time offering without eating-remnants.

sourceRefs.note: Rav Nachman's taxonomic disaggregation of the three cases

argumentFlow.label: Anonymous objection: blood-sprinkling ruling proves dchuya
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: A third proof: blood that became impure and was sprinkled - if done beshogeg (unwittingly), the service is accepted; if bmezid (intentionally), it is not accepted. If hutrah, why would intentional sprinkling of impure blood not be accepted?

sourceRefs.note: Anonymous objection (מיתיבי) from the blood-sprinkling baraita

argumentFlow.label: Anonymous answer: the blood-sprinkling baraita concerns an individual
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: That baraita was taught only about an individual's offering, which falls outside the communal hutrah/dchuya dispute entirely. It says nothing about the communal case.

sourceRefs.note: The Gemara's answer to the blood-sprinkling proof; unattributed in the raw text

argumentFlow.label: Anonymous objection: tzitz baraita explicitly includes tzibbur
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: A fourth proof: the tzitz effects acceptance 'for blood, flesh, and fat that became impure - whether unwittingly or intentionally, whether under compulsion or willfully, whether for an individual or a communal offering.' If tumas meit in tzibbur were simply permitted, the tzitz would have nothing to do for communal impurity - why is it listed?

sourceRefs.note: Anonymous objection (ת״ש) from the tzitz baraita; the strongest challenge on the daf

argumentFlow.label: Rav Nachman answers in two stages: an individual's offering, or non-fixed-time communal
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Nachman
argumentFlow.text: Two answers: (1) When the baraita teaches that the tzitz effects acceptance, it is teaching this about an individual's offering; a communal offering is fit even without the tzitz, simply because impurity is a permission (heter) for it. (2) Or, granting that the baraita does mean a communal offering, it is limited to offerings without a fixed time, for which hutrah's rationale does not apply.

sourceRefs.note: Rav Nachman's two-pronged answer to the tzitz proof

argumentFlow.label: New objection: which sin does the tzitz atone for?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: An objection is raised from the tzitz's own verse: 'Aaron shall bear the sin of the sacred things' (Exodus 28:38). Which sin can this mean? Not piggul - the Torah already states a piggul offering 'will not be accepted.' Not notar - the Torah already states notar 'will not be credited.'

sourceRefs.note: Objection opened from the tzitz's atonement verse

argumentFlow.label: By elimination the candidate is tumah - but the daf ends before the Gemara says so
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Having excluded piggul and notar, the only sin left unaddressed is tumah - but the Gemara's own text breaks off mid-sentence after the complete word 'הא' ('Hence...'), leaving the clause unfinished. Rashi notes explicitly that the comment is completed on 7b. What this implies for the hutrah/dchuya dispute is not stated on this daf.

sourceRefs.note: The daf's physical cutoff; Rashi: 'the comment is completed on 7b'

misconceptions.misconception: Rav Nachman is losing this debate - each answer is a step toward conceding dchuya.
misconceptions.correction: Rav Nachman holds hutrah (per the dispute stated on 6b) and Rav Sheshet holds dchuya; Rav Sheshet opens the challenge with the omer baraita, and three further anonymous objections continue pressing the same direction. Rav Nachman's answers narrow the scope of what still counts as a genuine test of hutrah, but each one is a defense of his position, not a concession to dchuya.

misconceptions.misconception: The 'be shrewd and keep silent' instruction supports hutrah, since the impure offering can proceed.
misconceptions.correction: Rav Sheshet uses it to argue for dchuya: the priest is told to seek a replacement first. Only when no replacement exists does the impure offering proceed. This is exactly the structure of dchuya: minimize where possible.

misconceptions.misconception: The daf concludes that the tzitz atones only for tumah.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara narrows the possibilities by elimination - piggul and notar are both excluded by their own pesukim - but the daf's text breaks off mid-sentence after the complete word 'הא', before stating which sin remains. Rashi notes this comment is completed on 7b.

Rav Nachman's disaggregation of 'bulls, rams, sheep' into three cases: par avodah zarah (no fixed time), Aaron's ram (individual), omer lamb (eating-remnants) - showing why none qualifies as a true communal-fixed-time offering

quizSeeds.question: Why does Rav Nachman concede that the omer offering must be performed in purity, without that concession counting against his hutrah position?
quizSeeds.answer: The omer has eating-remnants (the leftover minhah is eaten by priests). The requirement for purity derives from the obligation to eat the remnants in purity - not from the tumas meit rule for communal service.
distractors: The omer is an individual's offering, so the communal rule never applies to it
The omer has no fixed time, so it is not covered by hutrah
The omer is performed before the opening of the Temple service

quizSeeds.question: What three cases does Rav Nachman identify when he disaggregates 'bulls, rams, and sheep' in the meal-offering baraita?
quizSeeds.answer: Bulls = par avodah zarah (a communal offering, but since it lacks a fixed time, seeking a pure replacement is unremarkable and doesn't test the rule governing fixed-time communal offerings). Rams = Aaron's ram on Yom Kippur (an individual's offering, not communal). Sheep = the lamb accompanying the omer (has eating-remnants, so purity is required for that reason).

quizSeeds.question: The Gemara's final objection on 7a argues from the tzitz's own atonement verse. What two sins does it rule out by elimination, and why doesn't the daf name which sin remains?
quizSeeds.answer: Piggul is ruled out because the Torah already says a piggul offering 'will not be accepted'; notar is ruled out because the Torah already says notar 'will not be credited.' The Gemara's text breaks off mid-sentence after the complete word 'הא', before naming the remaining sin - Rashi notes the comment is completed on 7b.
distractors: The verse names tumah explicitly, so nothing needs to be ruled out
A gezerah shavah links the tzitz verse directly to a tumah verse on this daf
The daf states the conclusion, but only in Rav Nachman's name

alternateAngles.angle: Cumulative concessions and the erosion of hutrah
alternateAngles.text: Tracking the answers given on Rav Nachman's behalf reveals how sharply he delimits which cases genuinely test hutrah: only true communal sacrifices with a fixed time and no eating-remnants. That class is not marginal - the tamid and the festival musafim sit squarely inside it, and line 11's מאי לאו … דחג assumes as much. The angle worth pressing is not whether the class is empty, but whether needing four separate reclassifications to keep the disputed baraitot out of it is itself a strain on the position.

prerequisiteKnowledge: What makes an offering 'communal' and what makes it 'fixed time'
The tzitz's atonement function and its limits
The logical structure of elimination arguments: if not X and not Y, then Z

glossary.en: The bull offered when the entire community unwittingly commits idol worship (Numbers 15:22-26, Shelach Lecha), as Rashi cites here - distinct from par he'elem davar (Leviticus 4, the bull for a mistaken communal halachic ruling, subject of tractate Horayot). A communal offering but with no fixed time - brought only when the specific sin occurs. Rav Nachman cites its lack of a fixed time to explain why seeking a pure replacement is unremarkable here, so this case does not test the hutrah/dchuya question either way.

The golden frontplate worn by the Kohen Gadol, inscribed with the divine name. It effects acceptance for offerings that became impure. A closing objection on 7a argues by elimination that it cannot atone for piggul or notar (both excluded by their own pesukim); the daf's text breaks off before naming which sin remains, and Rashi notes the comment is completed on 7b.

An offering disqualified for a reason the Gemara treats as already fully excluded by its own verse: 'lo yeiratzeh' (it will not be accepted). Because the Torah has already foreclosed acceptance for this reason, the tzitz - whose function is to effect acceptance - cannot be operating on piggul, so piggul cannot be the sin the tzitz addresses.
Meat of an offering left after the permitted eating time. The Torah declares 'it will not be credited' (lo yechashev) - so the tzitz cannot remedy this disqualification either.

Be shrewd and keep silent. The pragmatic instruction to proceed with an impure offering when no replacement is available, without announcing the impurity. Rav Sheshet cites the existence of this instruction as proof of dchuya: the default is to seek a replacement, so the prohibition remains operative.

rashiTranslations.en: 'All corpse impurity in a community the Merciful One permitted' - as it is written (Numbers 9), 'any man who shall be'
'impure from a corpse shall perform the second Pesach': an individual is deferred to the second Pesach, but a community is not deferred. But
zavim, metzora'im, niddot, and yoladot, whose impurity issues out upon them from their own body, were not permitted,
and one who cohabits with a niddah is like a niddah. 'I concede where there are remainders for eating' - for although a communal offering
is offered in impurity, it is not eaten
in impurity, as we say in the chapter Keitzad Tzolin (Pesachim 77b);
and regarding a minchah from which a handful is taken, I concede
that we go back and perform it in purity, so that the
remainders may be eaten. 'And if there is only it' -
that he did not find another one prepared for this. 'What, is it not bulls'
'and rams of the Festival' - which are a communal offering and whose time is
fixed, and the minchah of the libations overrides impurity;
and yet it teaches 'he speaks and they bring another in its place',
which shows it is deferred-but-permitted for a community. 'A bull'
'of idolatry' - it is a communal burnt offering and requires
libations, in Shelach Lecha. 'Aaron's ram' -
of Yom Kippur. 'With the lamb that comes with'
'the omer' - as it is written (Leviticus 23), 'and you shall offer'
'on the day you wave the omer'; and that
'minchah of lambs' which it teaches does not speak of the minchah of
libations, for that is entirely burned, but of the minchah of
the omer itself that comes with it, from which a handful is taken
and whose remainders are eaten. 'Intentionally, it was not accepted' -
even though the tzitz effects acceptance, the Sages penalized him
so that the flesh should not be eaten; but the owners
have nonetheless been atoned for, so that non-sacred animals not be brought into the courtyard,
since by Torah law it is fit. And in any case we learn
from it that it is not a permission. 'For what does the tzitz'
'effect acceptance' - as it is written, 'and Aaron shall bear the sin of'
'the sacred things', that they be accepted for the owners. 'Willingly' -
it is included within 'intentionally', but alongside 'under compulsion' it is fitting
to teach 'willingly'. 'Whether for a community' - and since the
tzitz is needed to effect acceptance, learn from it that it is not a permission.
And what is the difference between an individual and a community? That for an individual,
bodily impurity is not overridden, since the tzitz does not
effect acceptance for bodily impurity; whereas for a community
bodily impurity is overridden for them, and not by means of
the tzitz. In any case we learn from it that since impurity of
the flesh, and offerings that go up, in a community require the tzitz
to effect acceptance, learn from it that bodily impurity
which is overridden for them is overridden only with difficulty, and however much we can return to purity we return.
'When it teaches that the tzitz effects acceptance, it teaches it about an individual' - and about a community it teaches its fitness, for even
a community's offering is fit, and not by means of the tzitz, but because it is a permission for it. 'And if you wish, say'
'about a community' - it refers to that as well, and it speaks of those offerings that have no fixed time, for which impurity is not
overridden for it, saying that the tzitz effects acceptance for them. 'The reading is: if the sin of piggul, it has'
'already been said, it shall not be accepted; and if the sin of notar, it has already been said, it shall not be credited.' And this
is its explanation: which sin can occur in an offering such that the tzitz effects acceptance for it, so that it be fit?
If the sin of intent outside its place, which is called piggul, as we say in Zevachim
(28a), 'this third one is outside its place', it has already been said in Kedoshim Tihyu,
'it is piggul, it shall not be accepted', and we established it as outside its place in tractate Zevachim. And if
the sin of intent of notar, where he intended at the slaughter to eat it outside its time, it has
already been said, 'the one who offers it, it shall not be credited', and we established it as intent outside its time.
'This' - the comment is completed on 7b.
